Worktrees, Branches & Publishing ​

A run that touches code accumulates its work on one branch per project, in one private git worktree per project, and commits locally. Nothing reaches origin until you explicitly publish.

One branch per run, per project ​

The branch name is derived from the run's title and the tail of its id:

ts
`saidi/run-${slugify(title)}-${runId.split('-').pop()}`

slugify lowercases, collapses everything non-alphanumeric to -, trims leading and trailing dashes, and truncates to 40 characters (falling back to change if nothing survives). So a run titled "Fix the checkout total" produces something like saidi/run-fix-the-checkout-total-4f2a.

The name is stable and deterministic, and that is the point: it is named after the run, not after each task, so every delegation in the run accumulates on the same branch instead of cutting a fresh one each time. Every project delegation passes it as newBranchName alongside reuseBranch: participant.branch, and if the deterministic name already exists (a first delegation after a crash or repair) it is reused rather than forked.

The branch a participant is on is tracked on the run's RunParticipant.branch record and captured the moment it is decided — before editing starts — so a process that dies mid-edit can resume the same worker session on the same branch. A branch that has been deleted out of band is cleared rather than handed forward as reusable.

Runs also pass keepEmptyBranch: true: a delegation that changed nothing keeps the run branch, because the branch is the run's shared context. Other callers tidy up an empty fresh cut.

Each project gets an isolated worktree ​

A repo has one working tree, so every path that touches it has to serialise on the repo lock. The old model checked the run branch out, edited, committed, and checked the base back out — which meant two runs on one project proceeded strictly turn by turn, and the checkout dance itself produced edits that vanished when another delegation restored the base.

Instead, each run gets its own git worktree per project: its own HEAD, its own index, its own files, sharing the repo's object store.

memory/runs/<runId>/repos/<project>/

This is a guarantee rather than a convention, because git refuses to check one branch out in two worktrees:

fatal: 'saidi/run-x' is already checked out at …

Cross-branch contamination becomes something the filesystem will not allow — and unlike an in-memory lock, that holds across processes. Two runs can edit the same file in the same repo at the same time, each committing only its own change, while the shared tree stays on its original branch and clean.

How the base ref is chosen ​

The base is resolved explicitly and passed to git worktree add, never inherited from whatever HEAD happens to be. resolveBaseRef tries, in order, the caller's preferred ref (the project's policy branch) then staging, develop, main, master — and for each name it prefers the remote-tracking ref origin/<name> over the local branch, because a stale local branch is worse than no local branch. If none exist it falls back to origin/HEAD.

Reading git symbolic-ref --short HEAD instead is how a repo under a staging-only policy produced a branch cut from main.

Creation, reuse, and hydration ​

ensureRunWorktree has a lock-free fast path: if the directory already exists and its HEAD is the run branch, it is returned with created: false. Otherwise it takes the repo lock and:

  1. Re-checks under the lock (a concurrent delegation for the same run may have won).
  2. Removes and re-creates any stale directory left by a crashed run — a half-created tree is never adopted — then runs git worktree prune.
  3. Resolves the base and runs git fetch origin --prune.
  4. git worktree add <dir> <branch> when the branch already exists, otherwise git worktree add -b <branch> <dir> <base>.
  5. Hydrates the tree with what git does not carry.

Hydration matters because a fresh worktree has no dependencies and no local config:

WhatHow
node_modulesA copy-on-write clone first (APFS cp -c, or cp --reflink=auto), falling back to a symlink. Never npm ci
.env, .env.local, .env.development, .env.development.local, .env.stagingCopied into every package root (repo root plus one or two levels, e.g. apps/*, packages/*)

A CoW clone gives each run a genuinely private tree, so two concurrent builds cannot fight over node_modules/.cache. A partial copy is deleted rather than kept — it type-checks as "installed" and then fails deep.

Uncommitted work survives between delegations: a second call for the same run returns the same path with created: false and the tree untouched.

When there is no worktree ​

runWorktreeFor returns null — and the caller falls back to the shared tree under the repo lock, exactly as before — in three cases:

  • the runWorktrees setting is off (it defaults on);
  • the project's policy is branch: current, which commits onto the base branch (git will not check one branch out twice, so current and worktrees are mutually exclusive by design);
  • git worktree add failed, most often because the branch is already checked out somewhere else. The half-created directory is removed and the run continues on the shared tree.

Worktree setup never fails a delegation outright: any thrown error also resolves to null.

Run work commits locally ​

Every run delegation calls runProjectWork with push: false. After the agent's edits:

bash
git add -A
git commit -m "<first line of the task, ≤100 chars>

(via Saidi)"

and the change note reads:

Committed on `saidi/run-…` (local).

The commit subject is deliberately the first line of the task, bounded — a full delegation prompt as a commit message is how planning prose ended up in a repo's history. The full task stays in the run thread.

If the agent committed the work itself, the tree is clean but HEAD moved; that is detected and treated as a real change rather than reported as "no changes were needed".

When the project policy declares a verify: command it runs here, on the branch, and its pass/fail is reported mechanically in the change note. See Project Policy.

Worktree + publish lifecycle ​

Publishing is a separate, explicit step ​

Pushing and opening a PR is not per-turn. It happens when you (or PRIME, via the publish run tool) ask for it — the same publishRunProject path backs both the tool and the CODE view's PUBLISH button, so both behave identically.

The branch to ship is chosen in this order: an explicit operator pick (CODE view), then the tracked participant branch, then the run's headline branch. With none of those you get a refusal telling you to make a change with delegate (mode work) first.

publishRunBranch then, under the repo lock:

  1. Resolves the PR base from the repo's real default branch — origin/HEAD — falling back to the scanned project branch, then main. The scanned value can be stale.
  2. Verifies refs/heads/<branch> still exists. A stale tracked branch fails fast with a way forward rather than pushing blind.
  3. Pulls the latest base (--ff-only when it is checked out, otherwise a fetch origin base:base) so the PR reflects current remote state.
  4. Refuses when rev-list --count base..branch is 0: "has no commits beyond <base> — nothing to publish yet."
  5. git push -u origin <branch>.
  6. Opens a pull request against the base.

Outcomes:

ResultMessage
Pushed + PR openedPushed `branch` and opened a PR: <url>
Pushed, PR not openedPushed `branch`; open a PR manually.
Push failedPush failed for `branch`: <last line of git output>

Either way the result is appended to the run thread as an event from the project.

The run branch and the project's default branch ​

The default policy is branch: new — a saidi/* branch cut from the base, with the PR opened against the project's default branch. branch: current commits straight onto the checked-out branch instead, and is guarded: if that branch is main, master, or the project's declared branch, the work is refused unless the operator explicitly approved it.

The CODE view reads git state per project participant: runBranch, baseBranch (the project profile's branch, or main), the actually checked-out currentBranch, whether the tree is dirty, the base..run commits, the base...run changed files, and the branch's PR looked up live with gh (capped at five seconds). When run and base are the same branch — a branch: current project — it says so explicitly and shows the branch's recent commits instead of a range.

Dirty trees and conflicting branches ​

SituationWhat happens
Shared tree is dirty before workThe delegation refuses: "⚠️ <project> has uncommitted changes. Commit or stash them first, then ask me again."
Shared tree is dirty, but the dirt is this run's own branch being resumedAllowed. After a crash killed a worker mid-edit, the dirt is the in-progress work; the commit phase sweeps it into the resumed change
Worktree is dirtyAlways allowed — the worktree belongs to this run alone, so the dirt is never another run's edits
The run branch is already checked out in another worktreegit worktree add fails; the run falls back to the shared tree under the repo lock
A remembered branch has been deletedThe run self-heals onto its stable run-branch name; if that name already exists it is reused, never silently forked
Work is cancelled mid-editUncommitted edits are stashed (saidi cancelled: <task>); a freshly-cut branch is deleted only if nothing landed and the stash succeeded
Switching the run's branch from the CODE view with a dirty treeRefused: "…has uncommitted changes — switching branches now could lose them."

One subtlety in the shared-tree path: after committing, the tree is restored to base — unless base is itself a saidi/run-* branch. That would be a previous run's leftover rather than a human's checkout, and switching onto it once yanked the checkout out from under a live sibling agent mid-verification. Staying on this run's branch is the safe default.

Because the shared tree is restored to base, anything that inspects the repo afterwards is looking at base, not at the work. That is why mechanical checks without a worktree run inside withBranchCheckedOut under the repo lock — see Verification & Evidence.

Cleanup ​

Worktrees are released when a run ends and when it is deleted.

  • releaseRunResources calls removeRunWorktrees for runs ending done or cancelled. Worktrees are kept on error so a failed run's tree can still be inspected.
  • Removal first reaps processes still running inside the directory. A dev server holds its cwd open; removing the directory under it would leave a live process serving files that no longer exist while still owning the port. What was stopped is reported into the run thread — a dev server that vanishes without a trace is indistinguishable from one that crashed.
  • Then git worktree remove --force, a direct rm -rf of the directory (some git versions refuse a dirty tree even with --force, and the directory is this run's alone), and git worktree prune.
  • The whole repos/ root is removed, which takes the hydrated node_modules with it — roughly 800 MB per project worktree, the bulk of what a finished run occupies on disk.
  • If the project left the registry mid-run there is no repo to hand the worktree back to; the directory and anything running in it are still cleaned up.

git worktree prune is what keeps the repo's administrative state honest after a crash. Without it a killed run leaves a registration behind and the branch it held stays "checked out" forever — which would turn the isolation guarantee into a permanent lockout of that branch.

The branch always survives. It is the deliverable, and publishing a PR still needs it. Deleting a run removes Saidi's record and (by default) its on-disk assets and workspaces; the git branches are untouched.
